newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia moves to curb speculation in economy.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia moves to curb speculation in economy.

text.p: Malaysia said on Friday it would take a pre-emptive strike against speculation in property and share buying to ensure the country's 10th year of sparkling economic growth was not derailed.
The central Bank Negara Malaysia announced the curbs at the release of its 1996 annual report, which showed the current account deficit has narrowed and economic growth has moderated.

The new limits on bank loans to the property sector and for financing share purchases, were "precautionary and prudential" and only affect those sectors deemed "less productive and speculative", it said in a statement
"These measures are primarily pre-emptive and prudential in nature," Bank Negara Governor Ahmad Mohamed Don told a news conference.

Under the new measures, financial institutions cannot devote more than 20 percent of their total loan portfolio to the property sector. The measures also restrict borrowing to speculate in the stock market, Ahamd said.
The strike against property speculation adds to curbs enacted in late 1995, which included hefty surcharges on foreign purchases and other real estate loan limits.
Ahmad said the economy would continue to face the cooling effect of tight money and fiscal policies introduced last year.
Analysts said the report contained few surprises but the credit tightening may negatively affect the stockmarket and the property markets.
"Overall, this could be negative on the stock market...," said Nizam Idris, analyst at research house I.D.E.A.
"It's bad news for the property market," said Victor Wan, senior analyst at South Johor Securities. "We expect more consolidation within the industry."

"The stock market should experience weakness firstly on property-related stocks and then for the broader market," Wan said. "There will be a gradual chain effect as the general contractors experience a slowdown. Cement, tile and steel manufacturers should also see a slow down."

Responding to international concerns, Malaysia in 1996 reined in galloping economic growth to 8.2 percent from 9.5 percent in 1995, reduced the current account deficit to 13 billion ringgit ($5.2 billion) from 18.7 billion ($7.53 billion) and kept the inflation rate checked at 3.5 percent.
But Ahmad said Malaysia cannot rest on its laurels because its open economy is vulnerable to external developments.

Bank Negara forecast gross domestic product to grow 7.8-8.2 percent this year, depending on whether exports pick up -- particularly in the electronics industry, which accounts for two-thirds of Malaysia's manufactured exports.
The report said slower exports growth could further widen the current account deficit this year, now projected at 14.8 billion ringgit against a 13 billion deficit in 1996.
The Bank said to maintain growth and keep inflation below four percent, it would continue its tight monetary policy, which means interest rates would remain at a relatively high level.

The growth in credit kept the supply of money high, with the broad M3 measure expanding by 22.7 percent last year from a peak of 27 percent in April, 1996. Ahmad said there were signs that M3 growth has showed some slowing this year with the central bank continuing to watch it closely.

"With the current account deficit (reduced) to around five percent of gross domestic product...They don't want to put too much pressure on the system," said Stephen Weller, director of strategy at Pesaka Jardine Fleming. "Therefore, we feel the chances of a rate increase are very limited."
"What they are trying to do is curb the inflow of speculative foreign funds, and if interest rates increase foreign funds inflows would increase," Weller said.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom 603-201-4813
